title: Modeling Viral Spread
question: How do host cells and contact paths affect the spread of a virus?

blocks.prompt: Required before observing spread: Which labeled contact would you close, and why? Predict how closing it might change the number of infectious people by round 3.
blocks.text: Closing CD may separate the two clusters and reduce the count by round 3.

blocks.prompt: Required before observing spread: What should stay the same in the open-network and one-closed-contact comparisons? How could another path reduce the effect of your chosen closure?

Closed contact: CD. Choice timing: Chosen before either network run.

Both networks have the same six people and contacts. A starts infectious: able to pass the virus on. Everyone else starts susceptible: able to become infected. The same three-round rule applies to both. Choose one contact to close before either run; only that link changes.
Provided possible contacts: A–B, A–C, B–C, C–D, D–E, D–F, E–F.
Student attached a particle at a host-cell receptor, then observed model-provided entry/copying/assembly/release.
This is an illustrated host-dependent process, not a measured particle yield. Written reasoning below provides evidence of the student’s explanation.
Source: deterministic teaching model. New infections use only the prior-round infectious set. Rounds on the same network are related time points.

blocks.prompt: Where can this model virus make new particles?
blocks.text:
Inside a suitable living host cell, using cellular processes and viral instructions.
Correct! Viruses do not have their own ribosomes. They use host-cell processes, and viral instructions and enzymes help produce new viral parts. Revised after feedback.

blocks.prompt: Which contact first allowed infection to reach D in the open network?
blocks.text:
C–D
Correct! At round 1, A can infect B and C. In the next round, C connects to D. Only people infectious before a round can transmit during it. Correct on first recorded check.

blocks.prompt: Does a contact always cause infection in real life?
blocks.text:
No. Certain transmission is a simplifying rule of this model.
Correct! The model makes transmission certain to isolate contact paths. Real outcomes depend on the virus, exposure and host, among other factors. Correct on first recorded check.

The cell view represents one simplified enveloped RNA virus, not every kind of virus. In this example, new particles gain envelopes while budding through the cell membrane. Entry, copying, assembly and release are shortened; cell and virus sizes are not to scale. Viral enzymes copy RNA, and host ribosomes make viral proteins. The network is an invented six-person model, not health data or a disease forecast. Every modeled infectious contact succeeds; real exposure does not always cause infection. A newly infected person can transmit only in the following round. Nobody recovers or gains immunity during these three rounds. Contacts stay fixed, and closing a link represents avoiding that contact rather than testing a product or treatment. A smaller count by round 3 does not prove permanent prevention. One network comparison cannot estimate real-world effectiveness.
